movedToNotes: Two problems pushed Seoul to act: first the Nanjido landfill, then Fukushima and the Seoul blackout in 2011, which led to One Less Nuclear Power Plant.
1977 to 1978: Nanjido, an island in the Han River, is joined to the mainland and becomes the city dump. It was easy to reach and far from downtown.
Two mounds about 90 m high. Korea had no modern treatment yet for the gas or the dirty liquid draining out of the trash, so methane and toxic gases leaked.
1993: the city decides to close the dump (some sources say dumping ended in 1992). 2002: it opens as World Cup Park. More on Nanjido on slide 14.
2011: Fukushima, then a blackout in Seoul the same year
Background today: Korea makes only about a fifth of its own energy (22.1% in 2024, 35th of 38 OECD countries)
OECD = a group of 38 mostly wealthy countries

movedToNotes: B1 · Name, date and place: Seoul Energy Dream Center, opened 2012 in World Cup Park, Mapo-gu, on top of the old Nanjido landfill. Korea's first zero-energy public building.
B1 · Designed by a German and Korean team led by Fraunhofer ISE, for the Seoul city government.
B1 · If asked about Gerkan Marg & Partners: some sites credit them, I couldn't confirm it.
B2 · The ground: the landfill waste cannot carry the building's weight.
B3 · So piles go down through the waste to solid ground, and the building sits on a reinforced concrete base plate.
B4 · The shape: square plan, three floors that get wider as they rise, each turned 45° (a pinwheel look with slanted outer walls). The shape is meant to cut energy demand.
B5 · The wings: wedge-shaped roof edges that shade the windows, shelter the entrance and hold solar panels.
B5 · White marble facade reflects sunlight (one source says about 60%).
B6 · Solar panels on the roof, the wings and a small patch of ground cover the full yearly demand, about 280,000 kWh. It stays connected to the grid. Geothermal does heating and cooling.
B6 · Over 70% less energy than a similar ordinary building. That is a reported figure.
B6 · Certified by KGBC (Korea's green building certification) and the Building Energy Efficiency Label. Envelope designed to Passive House standards.
B6 · Passive House is a German standard for very well insulated, airtight buildings that need very little heating or cooling.
B6 · The program: a public exhibition and education center about energy.

movedToNotes: B1 · Name, date and place: Nowon Energy Zero House (EZ House), Nowon-gu, Seoul. Korea's first zero-energy apartment complex. Finished September 2017, residents moved in from November 2017.
B1 · Net zero means it makes as much energy as it uses over a year. Say it aims for net zero. The reported figure is 75 to 80% of its own energy.

B2 · The exploded view: ordinary building parts, carefully layered. Bottom to top: geothermal field, structure, Passive House envelope (insulation, airtight layer, triple glazing), heat recovery ventilation, solar panels.
B3 · How it got built: a national research program run by MOLIT with Seoul and Nowon-gu. Point out who was involved: the national government, the city, the district, companies and universities.
B3 · August 2018: Building 102 became the first Korean housing to earn German Passive House certification.

Row 01: the Independent Budget Office (IBO) found that food waste pickup nearly tripled while fines were on, then fell about 43% after they stopped.
Row 01: NYC bins don't show you what you threw out, and there's no reward for cutting back.

elements.old: Seoul proved the carrot works at scale.
2 million TOE six months early. 1.68 million people enrolled voluntarily. Retrofits financed at 1.75%.
elements.new: 2 million TOE goal met six months early · 1.68 million Eco-Mileage participants · retrofit loans at 1.75%

elements.old: Seoul also proved the carrot has a ceiling.
It banned landfilling, failed to build the replacement, and the waste went 130 km to communities that didn't make it.
elements.new: Direct landfill ban from January 2026 · not enough incinerators · some trash sent about 130 km by road

elements.old: New York is running the opposite experiment.
The stick without the carrot — and about 63% of its buildings are projected to miss their 2030 caps.

movedToNotes: Seoul showed that incentives can work across a whole city.

Seoul also showed the limit. The landfill ban started before there were enough incinerators, so some trash now goes to private incinerators in Cheonan and Sejong, and Gangnam plans to send some to Cheongju.
New York leans on fines, and LL97 leaves the financing to owners.
Closing line, say as written: "If I had to pick one idea for New York, it would be the retrofit loans. LL97 already has the fines, and owners still need a way to pay for the work."
Distances, if asked: Cheonan about 85 km, Cheongju about 110 km, Sejong about 125 km in a straight line. The 130 km on the slide is the road distance reported by Seoul Economic Daily (October 2026).
Q&A: "Would you rather design under Seoul's loans or New York's fines?"
Q&A: "Seoul banned landfilling before it had enough incinerators. Is LL97 asking for retrofits faster than New York's workers and suppliers can do them?"
Q&A: "Lotte World Tower is LEED Gold at 123 floors. Nowon was designed for zero energy at 121 units. Which one does more for the climate?"
If asked about Nowon: it targets net-zero energy and reports about 75 to 80% self-sufficiency. Avoid the 100% energy cost claim; use up to 61% lower.
Q&A: "Composting nearly tripled under fines and fell about 43% after the fines stopped. How do you add a reward so fines don't hit low-income families hardest?"
Q&A: "Should we count all park space, or only park space within a five-minute walk?"
Q&A: "Cheonggyecheon took out a highway that carried 168,000 vehicles a day and the predicted gridlock never came. Why is that hard to act on here?"
